column1: Development|Which example mainly illustrates growth rather than a qualitative developmental change?|An increase in a child's height|A new strategy for solving a puzzle|Improved perspective-taking|Better understanding of rules|Growth concerns measurable physical change; development includes changes in functioning and capabilities.

Development|Why should teachers avoid assuming all children develop at an identical pace?|Development varies across individuals and domains|Every child learns only through rewards|Age alone fixes every ability|Environment has no influence|Development shows broad patterns but rates and experiences differ; instruction should respond to evidence from learners.

Development|Which statement best describes heredity and environment?|Both interact in development|Only heredity matters|Only the classroom matters|Neither has any effect|Inherited characteristics and experiences interact rather than acting as completely isolated explanations.

Development|Which practice supports child-centred education?|Planning activities around learners' needs and participation|Giving identical punishment to everyone|Preventing questions|Using only teacher monologues|Child-centred teaching makes learners active participants while the teacher provides purposeful guidance.

Development|A child solves a task with help but cannot yet solve it alone. Which concept is most relevant?|Zone of proximal development|Classical conditioning|Fixed intelligence|Maturation without experience|Vygotsky's ZPD concerns the difference between independent performance and performance with suitable guidance.

Development|What is scaffolding in learning?|Temporary support adjusted and reduced as competence grows|Permanent completion of all work by the teacher|Removing all challenging tasks|Ranking students by handwriting|Scaffolding supports a learner during a task and is gradually withdrawn as independent competence develops.

Development|Which task is associated with Piaget's idea of conservation?|Recognizing that quantity remains despite a change of shape|Remembering a password|Identifying a musical note|Running at a fixed speed|Conservation involves understanding that transformations in appearance need not change quantity.

Development|A young child assumes everyone sees the scene exactly as they do. Which term describes this?|Egocentrism|Reversibility|Metacognition|Scientific reasoning|In this developmental context, egocentrism means difficulty coordinating another person's perspective, not selfishness.

Development|What does object permanence mean?|Understanding that an object exists even when out of sight|Knowing every object's weight|Believing objects never move|Seeing all hidden objects directly|Object permanence is the understanding of continued existence without immediate perception.

Development|Which ability is especially associated with formal operational reasoning?|Reasoning about hypothetical possibilities|Only recognizing familiar faces|Only reaching for nearby objects|Only copying letters|Formal operational reasoning includes abstract and hypothetical reasoning; teaching still depends on the individual task and learner.

Learning|Which example illustrates learning through observation?|A pupil adopts a strategy after watching a peer model it|A plant grows toward light|A ball accelerates downhill|Water freezes overnight|Observational learning involves attending to and learning from a model, not merely physical change.

Learning|What is positive reinforcement?|Adding a consequence that increases the likelihood of a behaviour|Always giving punishment|Removing every classroom rule|Ignoring all behaviour|Reinforcement is defined by its effect on behaviour; positive refers to adding a consequence.

Learning|How does negative reinforcement differ from punishment?|It increases behaviour by removing an aversive condition|It always decreases behaviour|It means giving a low mark|It means publicly criticizing a child|Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to strengthen behaviour. Punishment aims to reduce behaviour.

Learning|What is intrinsic motivation?|Engaging because the activity itself is interesting or satisfying|Studying only for a cash prize|Working only to avoid a fine|Copying solely to gain a reward|Intrinsic motivation arises from interest or satisfaction in the activity rather than a separate external reward.

Learning|Which classroom practice is consistent with constructivism?|Eliciting prior ideas and helping learners test and revise them|Treating learners as empty containers|Forbidding discussion|Assessing only memorized definitions|Constructivist approaches connect new understanding with prior knowledge through active sense-making.

Learning|What is meaningful transfer of learning?|Applying understanding to a new relevant situation|Repeating the same sentence faster|Memorizing without application|Forgetting previous experience|Transfer occurs when knowledge or strategies are used beyond the exact setting in which they were learned.

Learning|What is metacognition?|Awareness and regulation of one's own thinking and learning|Only the ability to hear|Only physical growth|A fixed memory capacity|Planning, monitoring comprehension and evaluating strategies are metacognitive processes.

Learning|A learner says an answer is wrong but cannot explain why. What should the teacher probe?|The learner's reasoning and evidence|Only the speed of writing|Only the colour of the notebook|Only the learner's age|Probing reasons makes misconceptions visible and supports conceptual understanding.

Learning|Which activity encourages problem solving rather than mechanical copying?|Comparing multiple strategies for an unfamiliar task|Copying a solved answer ten times|Reciting without understanding|Removing all choice and discussion|Comparing strategies promotes reasoning about conditions, efficiency and justification.

Learning|Why can an error be useful during instruction?|It can reveal a learner's current model or misconception|It proves the learner can never improve|It makes feedback unnecessary|It always means carelessness|An error is evidence to interpret, not a diagnosis of permanent inability or lack of effort.

Assessment|What is the main purpose of formative assessment?|Using evidence during learning to improve the next steps|Only assigning a final certificate|Only ranking schools|Only recording attendance|Formative assessment guides feedback and instructional adjustments while learning is still in progress.

Assessment|Which example is primarily summative assessment?|An end-of-course test used to report achievement|An exit ticket used to plan tomorrow's lesson|A diagnostic discussion before a unit|An informal rehearsal with feedback|Summative assessment summarizes achievement at the end of a defined period; purpose distinguishes assessment types.

Assessment|Why is a diagnostic assessment useful before teaching a unit?|It identifies existing knowledge and specific gaps|It replaces the entire course|It guarantees every learner has identical needs|It eliminates the need for feedback|Diagnosis helps plan suitable starting points and targeted support.

Assessment|Which feedback is most actionable?|Explain your grouping rule and check it against the third example|You are bad at this|Wrong again|Try harder without any guidance|Actionable feedback identifies the issue and a concrete next step rather than labelling the person.

Assessment|What does a rubric describe?|Criteria and performance levels for judging work|Only the date of an examination|Only the classroom seating plan|A list of punishment rules|A rubric makes evaluation criteria and levels explicit, supporting consistency and feedback.

Assessment|What does validity concern in an assessment?|Whether evidence supports the intended interpretation and use|Only whether the paper is colourful|Only whether results arrive quickly|Only the number of questions|An assessment should support the inference being made. A spelling test alone cannot establish mathematical understanding.

Assessment|What does reliability mainly concern?|Consistency of measurement under relevant conditions|The amount of decoration|The school's location|The length of a student's name|Reliable measurement produces sufficiently consistent results; reliability alone does not ensure valid interpretation.

Assessment|Which practice supports self-assessment?|Learners comparing work with explicit criteria and identifying next steps|Learners assigning marks without criteria|Removing feedback|Making peers responsible for all grades|Self-assessment develops monitoring when learners understand criteria and use evidence from their work.

Inclusion|What is inclusive education primarily concerned with?|Removing barriers to participation and learning|Teaching only the highest scorers|Separating every learner permanently|Giving every learner the same support regardless of need|Inclusion addresses barriers through accessibility, support and participation in a shared learning community.

Inclusion|Which difficulty is most directly associated with dyslexia?|Persistent difficulties in accurate or fluent word reading|Only difficulty seeing colours|Only limited running speed|Only difficulty remembering faces|Dyslexia concerns reading-related difficulties; identification requires appropriate assessment rather than one classroom error.

Inclusion|Which difficulty is most directly associated with dyscalculia?|Significant difficulty understanding and working with numbers|Only difficulty pronouncing one word|Only hearing loss|Only difficulty drawing straight lines|Dyscalculia concerns numerical learning. Support should respond to assessed needs without labelling from a single task.

Inclusion|Which support can help a learner with low vision access a worksheet?|Accessible digital text or appropriately enlarged high-contrast print|Smaller faint text|Removing the task entirely|Publicly comparing the learner with classmates|Accessible formats improve participation while maintaining learning goals; suitable adjustments vary by learner.

Inclusion|How should a teacher respond to a gender stereotype in a textbook?|Discuss and challenge it using diverse examples|Present it as a biological rule|Prevent all discussion|Assign tasks only according to the stereotype|Teachers can help learners question stereotypes and see varied roles and capabilities.

Inclusion|A learner speaks a different home language. Which response best supports participation?|Use multilingual resources and connect familiar language with new concepts|Punish the use of the home language|Assume low intelligence|Require silence until perfect fluency|Home languages are learning resources. Language difference should not be treated as an intellectual deficit.

Inclusion|Why is a single score insufficient to describe a learner fully?|Abilities, contexts and assessment conditions are multidimensional|Scores always measure every trait|Scores never change|One test measures all future success|Different evidence is needed for different capabilities; one score cannot capture the whole learner.

Inclusion|What does differentiated instruction aim to do?|Adjust pathways and support while pursuing appropriate learning goals|Make goals meaningless|Remove all assessment|Give the same task in exactly the same way to everyone|Differentiation responds to readiness and needs through suitable tasks, resources and support.

Classroom practice|Which activity best supports collaborative learning?|A shared task with purposeful roles and individual participation|One learner doing everyone's work|Unstructured copying of answers|Preventing discussion|Collaboration involves interdependence and participation, rather than simply sitting together.

Classroom practice|Which teacher question best encourages explanation?|What evidence supports your answer?|Is the answer B?|Have you copied it yet?|Who can repeat my sentence fastest?|Questions about evidence and reasons reveal thinking and encourage justification.

Classroom practice|How should a teacher use a learner's alternative conception?|Elicit it and design evidence-based activities that test it|Ignore it permanently|Punish it immediately|Treat it as proof of dishonesty|Learning can involve revising an existing conception; carefully chosen examples help reveal its limits.

Classroom practice|What is remedial teaching best based on?|A diagnosed difficulty and targeted instruction|Repeating the entire syllabus identically|Public humiliation|Random extra worksheets without feedback|Remediation should address the particular barrier and check whether the support improves learning.

Classroom practice|Why should a teacher vary examples across contexts?|To help learners identify the underlying concept rather than surface features|To confuse learners deliberately|To remove every common feature|To eliminate the need for explanation|Varied examples and non-examples help separate a rule from incidental details.

Classroom practice|What is the strongest reason to use concrete materials in early mathematics?|To connect actions and representations with mathematical ideas|To replace reasoning permanently|To prevent symbolic work forever|To reward only fast learners|Concrete representations support understanding when teachers explicitly connect them to ideas and symbols.

Classroom practice|Which use of a portfolio supports assessment?|Selecting work over time and reflecting on progress using criteria|Storing unrelated photographs only|Recording only attendance|Hiding all earlier drafts|A portfolio can show development across tasks and revisions when selection and reflection are purposeful.

Adolescence|What is a constructive response to an adolescent exploring different identities?|Offer respectful guidance and opportunities for reflection|Treat every experiment as misconduct|Prohibit all independent thought|Assume every adolescent has the same experience|Identity exploration benefits from supportive relationships, boundaries and opportunities to reason about choices.

Adolescence|Which teacher response promotes a safe classroom during adolescence?|Address bullying promptly and encourage respectful participation|Ignore harassment as normal|Share private student information publicly|Mock uncertain answers|A safe environment protects dignity and supports participation without humiliation.

Adolescence|Why can peer relationships matter during adolescence?|They can influence belonging, identity and behaviour|They completely replace all family influence|They eliminate individual agency|They determine every examination score|Peers can matter significantly, but family, school, culture and individual circumstances also influence development.

Research|What distinguishes a hypothesis from an unsupported conclusion?|A hypothesis is a testable proposed explanation|A hypothesis is always proved true|A hypothesis needs no evidence|A hypothesis is simply a final mark|A hypothesis states a proposition that can be examined through evidence; results may support or challenge it.

Research|What is a sample in research?|A selected subset of the population being studied|Every possible future participant|Only the researcher's opinion|The title of a report|A sample is drawn from a defined population. Its selection affects what conclusions can reasonably be generalized.

Research|Why is informed consent important in educational research?|Participants should understand relevant information and participate voluntarily|It permits any undisclosed data use|It removes every privacy obligation|It guarantees a particular result|Ethical participation requires appropriate information and choice; consent does not remove other ethical responsibilities.

Research|Why should a researcher distinguish correlation from causation?|Association alone does not establish that one factor causes another|Every correlation proves causation|Causation needs no evidence|Correlated variables must be identical|Confounding or reverse causation can explain an association; causal claims need an appropriate design and evidence.

Learning|What is assimilation in Piaget's framework?|Interpreting a new experience using an existing schema|Changing a schema to fit contradictory evidence|Learning only through punishment|Forgetting every previous experience|Assimilation fits experience into an existing schema; accommodation modifies the schema when needed.

Learning|What is accommodation in Piaget's framework?|Modifying a schema to account for a new experience|Always repeating an unchanged rule|Only increasing physical height|Only copying a peer's gesture|Accommodation changes a mental structure when the existing one does not adequately explain experience.

Assessment|Why are several kinds of assessment evidence useful?|They provide a broader picture of learning than a single task|They guarantee every learner gets the same mark|They make criteria unnecessary|They prevent feedback|Combining observations, explanations and tasks can reveal different aspects of understanding.

Adolescence|An adolescent asks for more choice in a class project. Which response best supports growing autonomy?|Offer bounded choices with clear goals and responsibility|Remove every expectation permanently|Reject all choices solely because of age|Complete the whole project for the learner|Autonomy develops through meaningful choices, guidance and accountability, rather than either total control or absence of boundaries.

Adolescence|Why should a teacher avoid assuming that all adolescents develop at the same rate?|Development varies across individuals and domains|Every learner has an identical timetable|Age determines every ability exactly|One test measures every form of development|Physical, social, emotional and cognitive development need not progress uniformly or identically in every learner.

Adolescence|A learner seems confident with friends but hesitant in public presentations. What is the most appropriate interpretation?|Performance and confidence can vary by context|The learner has no knowledge in any subject|The learner must be deliberately dishonest|Confidence is fixed and cannot change|Context, familiarity and perceived social evaluation can affect participation; one behaviour should not define the learner globally.

Adolescence|Which classroom practice can reduce embarrassment when adolescents make mistakes?|Treat errors as information for learning and respond respectfully|Display a public list of the least capable learners|Mock incorrect answers|Prohibit every attempt without certainty|A respectful environment makes it easier to attempt challenging work and use feedback without fear of humiliation.

Adolescence|How should a teacher respond when peer exclusion is reported?|Listen, document concerns and use the school's safeguarding and inclusion procedures|Dismiss exclusion as always harmless|Blame the excluded learner automatically|Require the learner to solve every problem alone|Peer exclusion should be taken seriously and addressed through appropriate school procedures rather than public humiliation or unsupported conclusions.

Adolescence|Which arrangement makes collaborative work more accountable?|Clear roles, shared goals and evidence of individual contribution|One learner doing every task|No roles and no monitoring|Rewarding only the loudest participant|Structure supports participation and prevents group work from hiding unequal contributions or understanding.

Adolescence|Why can peer feedback be useful for adolescent learners?|It can expose alternative explanations and support revision when criteria are clear|Peers are always more accurate than every teacher|It removes the need to learn the content|It should consist only of popularity votes|Feedback is useful when specific, respectful and linked to evidence, rather than status or friendship.

Adolescence|A student disagrees with a classroom rule. Which response encourages reasoned judgment?|Invite reasons and discuss the rule's purpose and fair application|Treat every disagreement as proof of inability|End all discussion permanently|Change the rule randomly without explanation|Adolescents can practise examining reasons, consequences and fairness within clear expectations.

Adolescence|Which task especially supports hypothetical reasoning?|Predict outcomes under different stated assumptions and justify them|Copy a heading repeatedly|Count notebooks without interpreting anything|Repeat an answer without considering conditions|Hypothetical reasoning explores possible conditions and consequences while keeping assumptions explicit.

Adolescence|Why should abstract ideas still be supported by examples in secondary classes?|Examples can connect unfamiliar concepts to prior knowledge and reveal misconceptions|Adolescents never benefit from concrete representations|Examples replace all reasoning permanently|Every abstract concept is already understood at a fixed age|Age alone does not guarantee mastery; examples and varied representations help learners build and test understanding.

Adolescence|What is metacognitive monitoring during study?|Checking one's understanding and deciding whether a strategy is working|Only rereading without attention|Only counting study minutes|Assuming familiarity always means mastery|Monitoring lets learners identify gaps and adjust strategies rather than rely only on how familiar material feels.

Adolescence|Which study action best supports retrieval practice?|Attempt an answer from memory, then check and correct it|Look at the answer while copying every time|Highlight every word without selection|Avoid checking any response|Retrieval requires bringing information to mind; checking afterward helps correct errors and consolidate learning.

Adolescence|How does spaced study differ from cramming?|Study opportunities are distributed across time|Every topic is studied only once|All study occurs in one uninterrupted block|The learner never revisits material|Spacing provides repeated opportunities for retrieval and consolidation over time rather than one concentrated session.

Adolescence|Which goal is most useful for planning an adolescent learner's next study session?|Explain and solve three fraction-equivalence examples, then check errors|Become perfect at every subject instantly|Study without a purpose indefinitely|Never make any mistakes|A specific achievable goal names the capability and evidence, helping the learner plan and assess progress.

Adolescence|A learner mistakes fluent rereading for mastery. What would provide stronger evidence?|Explain the idea and answer a new question without consulting notes|Read the title more quickly|Increase the font size|Count highlighted sentences|Independent explanation and transfer reveal understanding more directly than repeated exposure alone.

Adolescence|What makes formative feedback actionable?|It identifies a gap and a feasible next step tied to the task|It labels the learner permanently|It states only a mark|It compares the learner's worth with friends|Actionable feedback directs an improvement and should be followed by an opportunity to use it.

Adolescence|Why is private feedback sometimes preferable for a sensitive performance issue?|It can protect dignity and support a focused conversation|It prevents the learner from receiving any feedback|It guarantees automatic agreement|It hides every assessment criterion|Respectful private discussion can address concerns without unnecessary public embarrassment; transparency about criteria remains important.

Adolescence|What is a mastery-oriented classroom goal?|Improve understanding and competence through practice and feedback|Prove classmates are less worthy|Avoid all challenging work|Focus only on appearance|Mastery goals emphasize learning progress; they do not remove standards or the need for evidence.

Adolescence|Which statement reflects a useful view of ability during learning?|Skills can improve with appropriate strategies, practice and support|Every difficulty proves a permanent inability|Effort alone guarantees success regardless of strategy|Feedback is never needed|Development requires effective methods and opportunities; effort matters but should be connected to strategy and evidence.

Adolescence|A learner repeatedly fails a difficult task. What is the best instructional next step?|Diagnose prerequisites and provide targeted support before further practice|Assign the same task indefinitely without feedback|Conclude the learner cannot improve|Remove all learning goals|Repeated failure can indicate gaps or unsuitable support; diagnosis should guide the next learning opportunity.

Adolescence|Why should assessment use more than one source of evidence when practical?|A single task may not capture understanding across contexts|Every observation is equally valid automatically|Evidence makes teaching unnecessary|All learners must submit identical answers|Several well-aligned observations can improve interpretation, while each source still needs appropriate criteria.

Adolescence|Which example is an access support rather than an unrelated lowering of the learning goal?|An accessible text format while retaining the reasoning objective|Awarding full marks without any work|Removing the concept from the task entirely|Scoring only handwriting in a reasoning task|Access supports help learners demonstrate the intended capability without irrelevant barriers.

Adolescence|How should classroom examples represent social and cultural identities?|Use varied respectful examples without presenting one group as inherently inferior|Use stereotypes as fixed explanations|Assume every family has identical resources|Exclude every unfamiliar context|Representation influences belonging and interpretation; examples should broaden participation rather than impose stereotypes.

Adolescence|Why should a teacher distinguish home-language proficiency from subject understanding?|Language demands can obscure what a learner knows|Using another home language proves low ability|Only one language can express reasoning|Content knowledge never depends on prior experience|A language barrier and a conceptual gap require different support; multilingual learners may understand more than one assessment format reveals.

Adolescence|Which practice can help a hesitant multilingual learner join discussion?|Provide preparation time and supportive ways to express reasoning|Require instant public responses in every case|Mock pronunciation|Ignore the learner permanently|Preparation and supportive participation options can reduce language-related pressure while preserving meaningful cognitive engagement.

Adolescence|What is a constructive purpose of classroom debate?|Examine claims, evidence and alternative perspectives|Win by insulting opponents|Repeat only the teacher's opinion|Avoid all disagreement|Debate is educational when reasoning and respectful response are evaluated rather than personal attacks.

Adolescence|Why should learners be asked to justify an answer?|Reasons reveal assumptions and understanding beyond the chosen option|Longer answers are always more correct|Every wrong option indicates identical misconceptions|Justification eliminates the need for subject knowledge|Explanations help distinguish sound reasoning from guessing and locate the specific source of an error.

Adolescence|What should a learner do when reliable evidence contradicts an initial explanation?|Revise the explanation while examining the evidence|Reject all evidence automatically|Change the subject permanently|Treat revision as proof of personal failure|Revising a claim in response to evidence is part of inquiry and does not require abandoning critical evaluation of sources.

Adolescence|Which digital-literacy question helps evaluate an online claim?|Who produced it, what evidence supports it and can credible sources corroborate it?|How colourful is the page?|How many exclamation marks does it contain?|Does it agree with every prior belief?|Source, evidence and corroboration are stronger criteria than visual appeal or agreement with expectations.

Adolescence|Why is sharing a classmate's personal information online without permission problematic?|It can violate privacy and cause harm|Online information can never affect anyone|Classmates have no privacy interests|Only adults need permission|Digital citizenship includes respecting others' privacy and using school reporting procedures for concerns.

Adolescence|What is a suitable response to suspected cyberbullying involving students?|Preserve relevant evidence safely and follow school safeguarding procedures|Encourage public retaliation|Forward the harmful material to everyone|Assume online harm is irrelevant|An appropriate response focuses on support, evidence and established procedures rather than escalating exposure or retaliation.

Adolescence|What is self-regulation in a learning context?|Managing goals, attention, strategies and responses while learning|Never experiencing any emotion|Always working without support|Only following a timetable blindly|Self-regulation includes planning, monitoring and adjustment, and can be strengthened through explicit instruction and practice.

Adolescence|A student is overwhelmed by a large assignment. Which support is most appropriate?|Break it into meaningful stages with checkpoints and feedback|Add unrelated tasks as punishment|Demand completion without clarifying requirements|Remove every opportunity to plan|Chunking and checkpoints help manage cognitive and organizational demands while keeping the overall goal clear.

Adolescence|Which classroom response supports emotional regulation during a disagreement?|Pause, acknowledge feelings and guide respectful problem solving|Insist emotions never occur|Reward the loudest insult|Humiliate both learners publicly|Regulation includes recognizing emotions and choosing constructive responses, rather than suppressing all feelings or escalating conflict.

Adolescence|Why should a teacher avoid diagnosing a learner from one classroom incident?|An incident lacks the context and expertise needed for diagnosis|One behaviour always proves a disorder|Teachers should ignore every concern|Diagnosis is identical to a low test score|Teachers can observe and refer concerns through appropriate channels without making unsupported clinical conclusions.

Adolescence|Which response is appropriate to a learner expressing persistent distress?|Listen respectfully and connect the learner with the school's appropriate support procedures|Promise that no adult will ever be informed under any circumstances|Dismiss the concern as laziness|Offer an unqualified diagnosis|Support should follow safeguarding procedures and professional roles; confidentiality has limits where safety obligations apply.

Adolescence|Why should adolescents practise evaluating consequences of choices?|It supports more deliberate decision making in real situations|It guarantees every future choice will be perfect|It eliminates the influence of context|It requires the teacher to choose every action forever|Considering likely outcomes, alternatives and values helps develop judgment while recognizing uncertainty and support needs.

Adolescence|What is perspective taking?|Considering how a situation may appear to another person|Agreeing with every opinion automatically|Ignoring one's own evidence|Assuming all people have identical experiences|Perspective taking supports understanding and communication without requiring uncritical agreement.

Adolescence|Which response to a harmful stereotype best supports critical thinking?|Ask for evidence, examine counterexamples and discuss its effects respectfully|Repeat it as an unquestionable fact|Ban all evidence-based discussion|Apply it to grade every learner|Stereotypes make unsupported generalizations; evidence and respectful examination help learners challenge them.

Adolescence|Why should participation expectations be explicit in a secondary classroom?|They help learners understand how to contribute and listen fairly|They remove the need for respectful conduct|They guarantee identical opinions|They permit only one learner to speak all year|Clear expectations can support inclusive discussion and make both speaking and listening responsibilities visible.

Adolescence|What is the purpose of a reflective learning journal?|Examine strategies, difficulties and next steps using specific evidence|Copy a mark without interpretation|Replace every assessment with decoration|List classmates' private details|Reflection is useful when it connects experience with reasons and planned changes rather than only descriptions.

Adolescence|How can a teacher scaffold a challenging explanation task?|Model the reasoning, provide prompts and gradually reduce support|Provide the final answer forever|Remove every challenge immediately|Use unrelated punishments|Scaffolding helps learners perform with support and move toward greater independence as competence develops.

Adolescence|Why should support be reduced when a learner can perform independently?|It encourages independent use of the skill|It proves the original support was useless|It removes the need to monitor progress|It means no future feedback is allowed|Support should respond to current needs; fading it allows learners to take over the reasoning and execution.

Adolescence|Which evidence best indicates transfer of learning?|Applying a principle appropriately in a new situation and explaining why it fits|Repeating the original answer verbatim only|Recognizing a page colour|Copying an example without understanding|Transfer requires identifying relevant relationships across contexts rather than relying on identical surface wording.

Adolescence|Why can comparing two solution methods deepen learning?|It reveals assumptions, efficiency and conditions of use|It proves every method works in every problem|It eliminates the need to solve either example|It makes answer accuracy irrelevant|Comparison is useful when learners explain similarities, differences and why each method is appropriate.

Adolescence|How should a teacher use students' questions during a lesson?|Treat them as evidence of interests, prior knowledge and possible gaps|Assume every question signals disruption|Ignore questions that reveal confusion|Answer only the most confident student|Questions can guide clarification and planning, while classroom routines help manage time and participation.

Adolescence|What does learner agency involve?|Having meaningful opportunities to influence and take responsibility for learning|Having no obligations or goals|Never receiving guidance|Only selecting the classroom wall colour|Agency combines voice and purposeful action with responsibility and support, rather than unrestricted choice alone.
